demographics.trauma_type: Unexpected or traumatic death of a loved one

Negative Appraisals.value: My reactions since the event show that I am a lousy coper
The event happened because of the way I acted
I should have protected others and I failed

issues.item: Contamination: I feel dirty or contaminated because of what happened
issues.explanation: For trauma involving the unexpected death of a loved one, contamination appraisals are clinically atypical and hard to reconcile unless there was a specific disgust/violation element to the death exposure. The other selected appraisals ('Bad Coper' and 'Self-Comparison') fit bereavement-related PTSD more plausibly, but 'Contamination' points toward a different trauma phenomenology (e.g., assault or abuse) and is not coherent with the provided trauma type/profile.

issues.item: Self-Comparison: Somebody else would not have gotten into this situation
issues.explanation: For trauma type 'unexpected or traumatic death of a loved one,' these two appraisals imply substantial personal responsibility for causing or entering the traumatic situation. That is hard to reconcile with an unexpected death unless there are special circumstances not reflected anywhere else in the profile. A clinician would question whether these items fit this trauma type as stated.

vignette:
For seventy-five years, Mariam had built a life on certainty. As a judge, she had presided over thousands of cases, her reputation built on an unwavering belief in order, accountability, and the idea that every outcome could be traced back to a deliberate choice. That framework shattered on a Tuesday afternoon eighteen months ago, when her forty-two-year-old son, Samir, died of a sudden aortic dissection while coaching his daughter's soccer practice. He had been healthy, or so everyone believed. The paramedics said it was over in minutes. Mariam was at the courthouse when her husband called; she remembered the way the polished wood of her desk felt against her palm as she gripped it, the impossible weight of the receiver against her ear.

In the weeks that followed, Mariam found herself unable to return to the bench. She told herself it was the paperwork, the formalities of death. But the truth, which she admitted only in the quiet of her sleepless nights, was that she had come to believe the event happened because of the way she acted. In the months before Samir's death, he had mentioned feeling "off" - a tightness in his chest, some fatigue. Mariam, in her characteristically pragmatic way, had told him to schedule a physical when he had time, that it was probably stress from his new job. She had not insisted. She had not driven him to the emergency room herself. She should have protected him, she now knew, and she had failed. She was certain of this, as certain as she had once been of the law. Her reactions since the event - the paralysis, the inability to make even simple decisions - only confirmed what she had come to believe about herself: that she was a lousy coper, a woman whose entire judicial composure had been a fragile performance that collapsed the moment it was truly tested.

This self-appraisal now colored every corner of her life. She had not returned to work. Her husband, David, found her in the study most evenings, staring at a framed photograph of Samir, her hands motionless in her lap. She did not attend her granddaughter's school play, because she was certain she would break down and ruin the evening for everyone. She stopped answering calls from her colleagues, convinced they must see her as weak, as someone who had failed the most fundamental duty of a parent. The only thing that felt real to her was the guilt, and she held onto it like a gavel, using it to judge herself more harshly than she had ever judged anyone in her courtroom. It was David who finally, gently, suggested she speak to someone. He found her one morning, still in her bathrobe at noon, staring at the blank television. "I can't do this alone anymore," he said. Mariam looked at him, and for the first time, she nodded. She was terrified of what a therapist might uncover - that her failure was even deeper than she imagined - but she was more afraid of staying frozen, a judge who could no longer preside over her own life.
